_notes.usage: Copy this file to config.json and fill in real values. config.json is gitignored-by-convention and should never be committed (it holds credentials).
_notes.model_path / paddleocr model dirs: model_path (the YOLO weights, e.g. best.pt) and alpr.paddleocr_det_model_dir/paddleocr_rec_model_dir/paddleocr_cls_model_dir are all resolved relative to the FOLDER config.json ACTUALLY LOADED FROM, not the code's location -- so by default everything lives together in one folder. Without these set, PaddleOCR silently downloads its models to the user's home directory (~/.paddleocr) instead -- including the cls (angle classifier) model, which PaddleOCR downloads unconditionally at startup even though use_angle_cls=false means it's never used for inference. Setting all three (as below) makes PaddleOCR look there first and download there if missing, keeping every model artifact next to config.json.
_notes.mqtt.trigger_enabled / http_trigger: Two independent, combinable trigger sources. mqtt.trigger_enabled (default true) subscribes to the VCA event topics below as before. http_trigger.enabled (default false) instead/additionally runs an HTTP server (served by waitress, a production WSGI server -- not Flask's dev server) that a camera's own alarm task (e.g. a Bosch dome's built-in 'HTTP notification' action) calls directly on a rule trigger, bypassing Genetec/MQTT for the trigger itself. MQTT stays connected and is always used to publish results either way -- disabling mqtt.trigger_enabled only stops it from subscribing. At least one of the two must be enabled. See the 'http_trigger' block below for its own settings.
_notes.http_trigger.port/threads: port must match whatever the camera's Alarm Task Editor HttpCommand is configured to send to (its Port(...) value) -- a mismatch means the request never arrives. threads is waitress's worker pool size; the default of 4 is plenty for this endpoint's workload (a handful of alarm hits per truck, each just a dict lookup + queue put). GET /healthz always returns 200 if the server is up, independent of ALPR's own health, for a process supervisor/load balancer to poll.
_notes.http_trigger SSL: If the camera's HttpCommand has SSL(false) (the default in Bosch's Alarm Task Editor), plain HTTP is all that's needed -- nothing else to configure. Only if a camera is set to SSL(true) would this need a certificate (e.g. a self-signed cert passed to waitress, or a reverse proxy terminating TLS in front of it) -- not set up here since it isn't needed for SSL(false).
_notes.snapshot: Every camera is pulled via a single HTTP GET to its snapshot endpoint (e.g. a Bosch dome's /snap.jpg), authenticated with HTTP Digest, using one common username/password for ALL cameras -- there's no per-camera override and no RTSP/Genetec path anymore (removed in favor of this). During a collection window the service polls this endpoint repeatedly (as fast as the HTTP round trip allows, or paced by poll_interval_ms) instead of decoding a continuous video stream. Chosen because trigger events here are trucks crawling in slowly, not fast drive-bys, so RTSP's much higher frame rate wasn't needed to catch a good shot.
_notes.snapshot.url_template: Default matches a Bosch FLEXIDOME 3000i/5000i's snapshot path: http://ip:80/snap.jpg. Confirm on your specific unit's web UI under RTSP/streaming (or HTTP) settings if snapshots fail or come back low-res.
_notes.alpr.expected_frame_width/height: Set to your camera's real sensor resolution (e.g. a 5MP camera is commonly 2592x1944) to catch the snapshot endpoint unexpectedly serving a lower-res image than the camera's actual sensor. Leave both null to disable the check.
_notes.logging.level: Text log verbosity: DEBUG / INFO / WARNING / ERROR. Independent of alpr.diagnostics_mode below, but diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting' forces this to DEBUG regardless of what's set here.
_notes.alpr.diagnostics_mode: 'basic' (default): saves the first fetched frame + its ROI crop, the selected plate crops, and the OCR-prep images -- fine for normal operation. 'troubleshooting': all of that PLUS every fetched frame (full image and ROI), the ROI annotated with every box the model returned (green=kept, red=rejected-by-size/position, orange=rejected-as-duplicate, with the rejection reason labeled), and every raw candidate crop saved the instant it's found rather than just the final best_samples -- and forces logging to DEBUG. Use this to see WHY, e.g., raw_cands stays at 0 (wrong ROI vs. camera framing? model detecting nothing at all vs. detecting boxes but all getting filtered out?). Generates a lot more files per event -- meant to be turned on temporarily while diagnosing, then switched back to 'basic'.
_notes.alpr.upper_half_fraction: A detected box is rejected as 'upper_half' if its vertical center sits above this fraction of the ROI's height (0.45 = reject anything in the top 45%). Meant to filter false positives from cab signage/mounting hardware above the real plate -- but if your camera's mounting angle puts the real plate legitimately high in the ROI, this will silently discard correct detections (confirmed via diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting': the model boxed the plate correctly but it was labeled upper_half). Lower it (e.g. 0.15) or set to 0 to disable the check entirely if that happens.
_notes.alpr.plate_crop_padding_pct: Expands each detected box by this percent of its own width/height (each side) before cropping for OCR, clamped to the ROI's bounds. Fixes a real observed failure: a slightly undersized YOLO box clips a character off the plate's edge -- confirmed via two adjacent, overlapping detections that each only captured half a plate ('HR47E' / 'E4812', sharing the boundary 'E', for what was actually 'HR47E4812'). Set to 0 to disable; raise it if plates are still getting clipped, lower it if crops start including too much surrounding clutter.
_notes.event_filter: Trigger events carry a VCA classification per detected object, e.g. Data.Object.Object.Appearance.Class.Type = {"#text": "Vehicle", "@Likelihood": 0.91}. Only events with a detection matching one of class_types (case-insensitive) at or above min_likelihood are queued for ALPR -- everything else (Person/Bicycle detections, low-confidence hits, events with no classified object) is discarded before a single snapshot is fetched. Tune min_likelihood against the values your camera actually reports (0.91 in the sample payload this was built from).
_notes.event_filter.class_types (disabling): Set class_types to an empty array, [], to disable this filter entirely and queue EVERY line-crossing event regardless of classification -- min_likelihood is then ignored too. Do not just delete min_likelihood or set it to 0/null while leaving class_types non-empty -- the event still has to match one of class_types first, so that alone would not stop filtering.
_notes.alpr.publish_no_valid_plate: true (default): every trigger gets an MQTT reply regardless of read success -- a NO_VALID_PLATE collection still publishes {..., "truck_number": null, "status": "NO_VALID_PLATE", ...} so a downstream consumer knows the event was processed, not just silence. The audit folder (result.json/event.json) is always written either way. Camera/system errors (CAMERA_UNREACHABLE, CAMERA_CONFIG_ERROR, FRAME_SIZE_ERROR, ERROR) are unaffected and always publish regardless of this setting. Set false to only publish actual successful reads.
_notes.mqtt enter/leave (filtering): Entering and leaving are two independent triggers, each its own MQTT subscription -- which rule/event types reach this service at all is decided by these topic filters (MQTT wildcards), not by any code-side filtering. Confirmed against real captured events for the SAME tracked object (ObjectId) a few seconds apart: enter_subscribe_topic matches 'Camera_Events/AR-H6/onvif-ej/RuleEngine/LineDetector/Crossed/&1/Entering field 2' (event_type=LineDetector; this same topic shape also covers plain 'Crossing line N' rules), and leave_subscribe_topic matches 'Camera_Events/AR-H6/onvif-ej/RuleEngine/ObjectTrack/Aggregation/&1/Leaving field 3' (event_type=ObjectTrack) -- '+' matches exactly one topic segment, '#' matches all remaining segments (only valid at the end, absorbs the varying '&1/<free text>' suffix). The two are structurally distinct (LineDetector/Crossed vs ObjectTrack/Aggregation) so there's no overlap between them.
_notes.mqtt enter/leave (results): Each direction publishes to its own topic (enter_result_topic_prefix/<bay> or leave_result_topic_prefix/<bay>) with a lean payload -- bay, direction, truck_number, confidence, status, event_time/ocr_time -- so a downstream gate/dock system can subscribe to entries and exits separately without parsing the fuller record. The complete detail (every OCR read, collection stats, rejection reasons) is still written to the audit folder's result.json regardless.
_notes.mqtt.bay_segment_index: 0-based position of the bay name within the subscribe topics, e.g. 1 for 'Camera_Events/<bay>/...'. Shared by both enter and leave since they use the same layout; adjust if yours differs.
_notes.bay_monitor: A separate, optional feature from the enter/leave ALPR pipeline above -- off by default (enabled: false). Continuously round-robins every enabled camera (independent of MQTT/HTTP triggers) looking for presence, reusing the ALPR plate model as a cheap 'something's there' signal with no filtering. Once a bay shows a detection it's 'zoomed in': every classify_interval_sec (default 60s) a frame is sent to a local Ollama-hosted vision model and the reply (one of status_values) is published to mqtt.bay_status_topic_prefix + '/<bay>'. After empty_debounce_count consecutive 'empty' replies it reverts to baseline scanning. ollama_model has NO working default -- it must be set to a vision-capable model tag you've actually pulled locally (`ollama pull <tag>`), and the service fails fast at startup if enabled without one set, rather than silently misclassifying everything.
_notes.bay_monitor.baseline_scan_interval_ms: Pacing between each camera checked in the round-robin (applies whether or not anything was found) -- keeps the scanner from hammering every camera back-to-back with zero gap. Does not apply to the classify_interval_sec cadence of a zoomed-in bay's LLM calls, which is separately paced.
_notes.bay_monitor.reference_images: Optional few-shot exemplars sent alongside every classification call, e.g. [{"path": "reference_images/empty.jpg", "label": "empty"}, {"path": "reference_images/door_open.jpg", "label": "occupied (bay door open)"}]. Paths resolve relative to config.json's directory, like model_path. Loaded once at startup, not re-read per call -- a missing file is logged and skipped, not fatal. Helps most on real ambiguous cases a text-only prompt undersells, e.g. an open bay/cargo door that can otherwise get misread as empty or throw off the model.
_notes.bay_state_engine: Off by default; depends entirely on bay_monitor also being enabled (fails startup otherwise). When on, it becomes the authority for enter/leave direction and timing INSTEAD of the MQTT/HTTP trigger source: bay_monitor's own empty->occupied transition enqueues an ALPR read via the normal Worker pool, and (unlike a one-shot trigger) keeps retrying every time bay_monitor reclassifies the bay as still occupied, until a read actually succeeds -- so a bad read caused by e.g. a bay/cargo door being open doesn't cost the whole visit's identity, just that one attempt. occupied->empty then publishes the leave result using whatever plate got confirmed at ANY point during the stay (there's no fresh camera read at that instant to attempt, since 'empty' means the truck's no longer in frame). If mqtt.trigger_enabled or http_trigger.enabled are ALSO on at the same time, both paths independently decide enter/leave for the same bays -- a startup warning (not a hard failure) flags this, since it usually means redundant or conflicting publishes; turn the old trigger(s) off if bay_state_engine is meant to be the sole source of truth. State is in-memory only -- a restart loses any truck currently mid-visit.

bay_monitor.classification_prompt: You are monitoring a truck loading dock bay through a fixed security camera. Classify the current activity into EXACTLY ONE of these words: empty, occupied, unloading, loading, idle. 'empty' = no truck present. 'occupied' = a truck is present but no cargo movement is visible. 'unloading' = cargo is visibly being removed from the truck. 'loading' = cargo is visibly being loaded onto the truck. 'idle' = a truck is present, not actively loading or unloading (e.g. waiting, doors closed, driver break). Respond with only the single classification word, nothing else.
